pr_title: [Merged by Bors] - Added Ref to allow immutable access with change detection
pr_body:
# Objective

- Fixes #7066 

## Solution

- Split the ChangeDetection trait into ChangeDetection and ChangeDetectionMut
- Added Ref as equivalent to &T with change detection

---

## Changelog

- Support for Ref which allow inspecting change detection flags in an immutable way

## Migration Guide

- While bevy prelude includes both ChangeDetection and ChangeDetectionMut any code explicitly referencing ChangeDetection might need to be updated to ChangeDetectionMut or both. Specifically any reading logic requires ChangeDetection while writes requires ChangeDetectionMut.

use bevy_ecs::change_detection::DetectChanges -> use bevy_ecs::change_detection::{DetectChanges, DetectChangesMut}

- Previously Res had methods to access change detection `is_changed` and `is_added` those methods have been moved to the `DetectChanges` trait. If you are including bevy prelude you will have access to these types otherwise you will need to `use bevy_ecs::change_detection::DetectChanges` to continue using them.
pr_comments: I did not implement `ResRef`'s SystemParam trait because I wanted feedback on this implementation. Most notably I wanted to ensure that the splitting of the `ChangeDetection` trait was a worthwhile breaking change.
A long time ago, this existed: https://docs.rs/bevy/0.4.0/bevy/ecs/struct.Ref.html. I think it was removed in the ecs rewrite in 0.5.
`Ref<'a, T>` was what is now covered by `&'a T` directly. This simply reintroduces it to cover when you need access to change tracking information. (I totally chose the name based on that one though)
I definitely think `Ref` is the right name here: there's a clear parallel with `Mut`.

> I definitely think `Ref` is the right name here: there's a clear parallel with `Mut`.

I don't necessarily disagree, but I want to note that these aren't exactly comparable. `Mut<T>` is a wrapper type that automagically replaces `&mut T` when used in a worldquery, whereas `Ref<T>` is a type that you'd have to explicitly name. This makes the name feel more arbitrary IMO, but I am pending a better suggestion.

I am fine with renaming Ref, I only chose it since I remembered that was what it used to be called.

Side note I moved Res into change_detection, it doesn't impact anything (ResMut has been there since before this PR) but it allowed me to steal the macros.

Also I made Res use Ticks in a previous commit. Both changes aren't important but they felt right from a consistency standpoint.

> Both changes aren't important but they felt right from a consistency standpoint.

I agree with this.

Should I leave `DetectChanges` as a mut thing and make the other methods not be based on a trait? I guess that matches the current.

It felt a little arbitrary but if it is better UX I am fine with it.
That's my personal preference, but you can wait for other opinions if you want, of course.

Doesn't this make `ChangeTrackers` obsolete? The current access model cannot differentiate between a change tick read and a component read, and the compiler will optimize out the unused reference, so I don't see a reason why we need `ChangeTrackers<T>` when we have `Ref<T>`.

review_comments: This description feels too broad: this is only for the Mut form.
All of this is unchanged, git just got confused because I put the new DetectChanges first.
This explanation was very useful, we either need to keep it or link to `DetectChangeMut`.
I didn't think explaining how to bypass change detection on a type that can't cause change detection was the right location.

Yeah, I agree there! But we should link to the subtrait in these docs: it's hard discover them otherwise.

I also think that mentioning that "change detection works via DerefMut" is important information.
I think there is a comment pointing towards DetectChangesMut now to point that (I used ResMut as an example too)

IMO putting the SAFETY comment between the let and unsafe block is ugly but rustfmt won't have it any other way.

The only other solve here would be to see if lifting the `self.last_change_tick()` into a local variable got the line length below the limit which didn't seem worth it.
